title: Interfaces

notes: The interface lists what every damageable thing must have, with no code.
Crate and Player both sign the contract with `: IDamageable`, but each does it its own way.
The list's type is IDamageable, so it can hold both kinds.
The loop only knows the interface; it never asks what the real class is.

exercises.title: Things that can be hurt
exercises.prompt:
The interface IDamageable is given. Write:
- class Crate : IDamageable, constructor Crate(int health). TakeDamage lowers Health by the amount, never below 0. IsDestroyed is true at 0.
- class ArmoredWall : IDamageable, constructor ArmoredWall(int health, int armor). Each hit is reduced by Armor first (a hit smaller than the armor does nothing), never below 0 health.
- In static class Combat, int Explode(List<IDamageable> targets, int damage): hit every target once, return how many are destroyed afterwards.

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var c = new Crate(10); c.TakeDamage(4); return c.Health + " " + c.IsDestroyed; }))()
tests.name: a crate takes damage

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var w = new ArmoredWall(50, 5); w.TakeDamage(20); w.TakeDamage(3); return w.Health.ToString(); }))()
tests.name: armor soaks part of each hit

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var list = new List<IDamageable> { new Crate(10), new Crate(30), new ArmoredWall(12, 2) }; return Combat.Explode(list, 14) + " " + list[1].Health; }))()
tests.name: explosion hits everything

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { IDamageable c = new Crate(5); c.TakeDamage(100); return c.Health + " " + c.IsDestroyed; }))()
tests.name: never below zero

hints: public class Crate : IDamageable { public int Health { get; private set; } ... }
ArmoredWall: Health = Math.Max(0, Health - Math.Max(0, amount - Armor));
Explode: foreach (var t in targets) t.TakeDamage(damage); return targets.Count(t => t.IsDestroyed);

exercises.title: A sortable leaderboard
exercises.prompt:
Make Score implement IComparable<Score> so that list.Sort() puts the HIGHEST Points first, and for equal points the FEWER Seconds first. A null 'other' sorts after (return -1).
Then write Leaderboard.Top(List<Score> scores, int n): the Player names of the best n, in order. Don't change the list you were given (sort a copy).

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var s = new List<Score> { new("Juma", 40, 10), new("Amina", 50, 30), new("Wanjiru", 50, 20) }; s.Sort(); return string.Join(",", s.Select(x => x.Player)); }))()
tests.name: ties go to the faster player

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var s = new List<Score> { new("A", 10, 5), new("B", 30, 9) }; Leaderboard.Top(s, 1); return s[0].Player; }))()
tests.name: the original list is untouched
tests.hint_if_fail: Sort a copy: var copy = new List<Score>(scores);

tests.name: asking for more than there are

hints: Higher first means comparing the other way round: other.Points.CompareTo(Points).
If that isn't 0, return it. Otherwise return Seconds.CompareTo(other.Seconds).
Top: var copy = new List<Score>(scores); copy.Sort(); return copy.Take(n).Select(s => s.Player).ToList();

exercises.title: Stock alerts (program to an interface)
exercises.prompt:
INotifier is given. Write two classes that implement it, each adding one line to Sent:
- SmsNotifier: "SMS to {to}: {message}", but an SMS message longer than 30 characters is cut to its first 30.
- EmailNotifier: "EMAIL to {to}: {message}".
Then finish StockAlert.Check(medicine, count, minimum, contact): if count < minimum, send "Low stock: {medicine} ({count} left)" to contact through the notifier it was given and return true; otherwise return false. A negative count throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException.

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var sms = new SmsNotifier(); var alert = new StockAlert(sms); bool a = alert.Check("Zinc", 4, 10, "Amina"); bool b = alert.Check("Zinc", 40, 10, "Amina"); return a + " " + b + " | " + string.Join(";", sms.Sent); }))()
tests.expect: True False | SMS to Amina: Low stock: Zinc (4 left)
tests.name: sms alert

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var mail = new EmailNotifier(); new StockAlert(mail).Check("Paracetamol", 2, 5, "clinic@mail"); return mail.Sent[0]; }))()
tests.expect: EMAIL to clinic@mail: Low stock: Paracetamol (2 left)
tests.name: email alert

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { var sms = new SmsNotifier(); sms.Send("Juma", "This message is far too long for one SMS"); return sms.Sent[0]; }))()
tests.expect: SMS to Juma: This message is far too long f
tests.name: long SMS is cut to 30

tests.call: ((Func<string>)(() => { INotifier n = new EmailNotifier(); new StockAlert(n).Check("Zinc", 10, 10, "x"); return n.Sent.Count.ToString(); }))()
tests.name: exactly the minimum is fine

hints: public class SmsNotifier : INotifier { public List<string> Sent { get; } = new(); public void Send(string to, string message) { ... } }
Cut a long SMS: if (message.Length > 30) message = message.Substring(0, 30);
StockAlert never says 'SMS' or 'email': it only calls notifier.Send(contact, ...). That's the point.

choices: A list of members a class promises to have
quiz.why: It's the contract; classes supply the code.

quiz.q: You add a new Barrel : IDamageable. What changes in the explosion code that loops over List<IDamageable>?
quiz.why: Code written against the interface works for every new implementer.

quiz.q: Which CompareTo sorts the HIGHEST points first?
quiz.why: Swapping the sides reverses the order.

quiz.q: Why does StockAlert take an INotifier instead of an SmsNotifier?
choices: So it works with any sender, including a fake one in tests
quiz.why: Programming to an interface keeps it flexible and testable.

quiz.q: How many interfaces can one C# class implement?
choices: None if it has a base class
quiz.why: One base class, but many interfaces.

cards.a: public interface IDamageable { void TakeDamage(int amount); }
negative: this first, 0: tie, positive: other first

explain: Explain what 'programming to an interface' means, with an example from a game or an app you'd like to build.
